lesson.title: Naming Triangles: Sides and Corners

steps.say: Hi friend, it's Ms. Yuanyuan! Yesterday I walked over a bridge in Vancouver and looked up at the metal bars. They were full of triangles! Builders love triangles because they don't wobble. But if I want to phone my friend and describe one, saying just "a triangle" isn't enough. Which triangle? So today we learn how to give every triangle its proper name.

visual.caption: A triangle inside a bridge — but what kind?

steps.say: Every triangle gets two names, like a first name and a last name. The first name comes from its sides. If all three sides are different lengths, we call it scalene. If exactly two sides are equal, we call it isosceles. And if all three sides are the same, we call it equilateral. Equal sides, equilateral — the word even sounds like equal!

visual.caption: Equilateral: 6 cm, 6 cm, 6 cm — all sides equal

steps.say: The second name comes from the corners, which we call angles. A perfectly square corner, like the corner of your math notebook, is ninety degrees. If a triangle has one square corner, it's a right triangle. If one corner is wider than a square corner, it's obtuse. And if all three corners are smaller than a square corner, it's acute. Remember, obtuse is the big open one, acute is the small sharp one.

visual.caption: Ninety degrees — a perfect square corner

steps.say: Let's try one together. Imagine a sailboat out on Okanagan Lake. Its sail has two sides of five metres each and a bottom edge of eight metres. First name: two sides are equal, so it's isosceles. Now the corners. The two bottom corners are each about thirty-seven degrees, and the top corner is about one hundred six degrees. Let's check: thirty-seven plus thirty-seven plus one hundred six is one hundred eighty. Perfect, because the three angles of every triangle always add to one hundred eighty degrees.

visual.caption: The sail: sides 5 m, 5 m, base 8 m

steps.say: Now the last name. Is any corner wider than a square corner? Yes — one hundred six degrees is bigger than ninety degrees, so that top corner is wide and open. That makes it obtuse. So the full name of our sail is an isosceles obtuse triangle. Two names, one from the sides, one from the biggest angle.

visual.caption: 106 degrees — wider than square, so obtuse

steps.say: Here's a slightly harder one. I'm cutting a triangle of plywood for a shelf bracket. The sides measure three centimetres, four centimetres, and five centimetres. All three sides are different, so its first name is scalene. Its corners measure about thirty-seven degrees, about fifty-three degrees, and exactly ninety degrees. Thirty-seven plus fifty-three plus ninety is one hundred eighty. There's a square corner in there, so its last name is right. It's a scalene right triangle.

visual.caption: Sides 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm — one square corner

steps.say: Now here's the tricky part that fools lots of kids. If I pick up that plywood bracket and flip it upside down, or tip it sideways, or spin it around — did any side get longer? Did any corner get wider? Nope! Not one bit. So it is still a scalene right triangle. A triangle's name never changes just because it's turned. Names come from measurements, not from which way it's pointing.

visual.caption: Same triangle, just turned — still scalene and right

steps.say: One more lovely one to finish. Think of a slice of Nanaimo bar cut so all three sides are six centimetres. All sides equal, so it's equilateral. And here's the magic: an equilateral triangle always has three sixty degree corners, because sixty plus sixty plus sixty is one hundred eighty. Every corner is smaller than ninety, so it's also acute. Equilateral triangles are always acute — always!

visual.caption: Every corner of an equilateral triangle is 60 degrees

lesson.answer: Give every triangle two names: one from its sides (scalene, isosceles, equilateral) and one from its biggest angle (acute, right, obtuse) — and turning it never changes either name.

practice.question: A triangular flower bed at a Surrey community garden has sides of 6 metres, 8 metres, and 10 metres. Its angles measure about 37 degrees, about 53 degrees, and exactly 90 degrees. What are the two names of this triangle?
practice.answer: It is a scalene right triangle. Scalene because all three sides are different lengths (6 m, 8 m, 10 m), and right because one angle is exactly 90 degrees. Check: 37 + 53 + 90 = 180 degrees. Even if the gardener rotated the whole bed, the name would stay the same.
